## Overview

The Crow, whose autonym is *Apsáalooke*, are Native Americans living primarily in southern Montana. Their federally recognized tribe is the Crow Tribe of Montana, whose Crow Indian Reservation lies in the south-central part of the state. The reservation is established south of Billings, Montana, and the tribal headquarters are at Crow Agency, Montana. The Crow are a Plains tribe whose language belongs to the Missouri River Valley branch of the Siouan languages. Of the 14,000 enrolled tribal citizens, an estimated 3,000 spoke the Crow language in 2007. Historically, the Crow lived in the Yellowstone River valley, extending from present-day Wyoming through Montana into North Dakota. Their culture developed through hunting, gathering, farming, horse use, river-valley settlement, intertribal relations, and adaptation to the nomadic lifestyle of the Plains Indians.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Tipis** — Crow camps included tipis, which were described as perishable kinds of homes.

**Robes** — Crow people traded surplus robes and skin at Fort Sarpy (II) near the mouth of the Bighorn River from 1857 to 1860.

**Green blanket** — After Crow chief Long Horse was killed in 1875, his body was wrapped in a green blanket.

### Clothing & dress

The sources provide little information about everyday Crow clothing. They state that Crow hunters used a wolf-pelt disguise when stalking bison on foot, and that Crow people traded robes and skin at Fort Sarpy (II). After the death of Long Horse in 1875, his body was wrapped in a green blanket and placed in a tipi, with his face painted.

### Architecture

Before 1700, the Crow used dog travois for carrying goods. In the period after leaving Hidatsa villages, some Crow selected a site for a single earth lodge on the lower Yellowstone River, while most families lived in tipis or other perishable kinds of homes. The sources identify a “proto-Crow” archaeological site in present Montana as the Hagen site.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

They mention arrows, lances, bullets, dog travois, a pipe-hatchet, and a medicine doll. A Crow medicine doll was given to a poor Arapaho at a Sun Dance before 1765; the Arapaho later made a duplicate, and the Kiowas used it during the Sun Dance as one of their most powerful tribal medicines.

### Jewelry & body adornment

They state that Crow woman Pretty Shield remembered Crow mourning for Long Horse, and that mourners brought the dead bodies back to camp with their hair cut off and their fingers and faces cut.

## Music & performance

The sources mention the Sun Dance as a Crow performance and ritual context. Before 1765, a poor Arapaho attended a Crow Sun Dance, where a Crow with power gave him a medicine doll. During a later Sun Dance, some Crow stole the figure back to keep it in the tribe. The Arapaho eventually made a duplicate, and the Kiowas continued to use the figure during their Sun Dance.

The sources also describe the Crow Fair, which began after the Crow organized a gathering in 1918 to display their culture and invited members of other tribes. The Crow Fair is celebrated yearly on the third weekend of August, with wide participation from other tribes. No musical instruments, song genres, musical forms, performance techniques, or named Crow compositions are identified.

## Dance & theatre

The sources name the Sun Dance and state that a medicine doll associated with the Crow was used during the Kiowa Sun Dance.

## Festivals & rituals

The Crow organized a gathering in 1918 to display their culture and invited members of other tribes. This gathering developed into the Crow Fair, which is celebrated yearly on the third weekend of August and has wide participation from other tribes.

The sources also describe the Sun Dance. Before 1765, a poor Arapaho attended a Crow Sun Dance, where he received a medicine doll from a Crow with power. The figure was later taken back by some Crow so that it would remain in the tribe. The Kiowas continued to use a duplicate during their Sun Dance and credited the Crow tribe with the origin of their sacred Tai-may figure.

Crow oral history also records the vision of No Intestines, who led his band on a long migratory search for sacred tobacco before the Mountain Crow settled in southeastern Montana. A vision by Plenty Coups, when he was a boy, was interpreted by tribal elders as meaning that whites would become dominant over the country and that the Crow would need to remain on good terms with them to retain their land.

## Foodways

The main food source for the Crow was the American bison. Before horses were used, hunters stalked bison on foot, sometimes using a wolf-pelt disguise, and killed them with arrows or lances. After horses became available, riders could panic a herd into a stampede and kill selected animals with arrows, bullets, or lances.

The Crow also hunted bighorn sheep, mountain goats, deer, elk, bear, and other game. Buffalo meat was roasted or boiled in a stew with prairie turnips. The rump, tongue, liver, heart, and kidneys were considered delicacies. Dried bison meat was ground with fat and berries to make pemmican. Wild edibles were also gathered and eaten, including elderberries and wild turnip.

The Crow formerly cultivated crops and hunted bison in settled villages before moving farther west.

## Oral tradition & literature

Apsáalooke oral history describes the Bilapiluutche, or “Beaver Dries its Fur,” as a fourth group that may have merged with the Kiowa in the second half of the 17th century. The sources also preserve traditions concerning the division of the Crow into groups, including the Ashalaho, Binnéessiippeele, Eelalapito, and Bilapiluutche.

Crow history includes the vision of No Intestines, who searched for sacred tobacco and led his band westward, and the vision of Plenty Coups, which tribal elders interpreted as a warning about the future dominance of whites. The sources also record the Crow account of a Crow medicine doll that became associated with the Kiowa Sun Dance and the sacred Tai-may figure.

## Language & religion

The Crow language belongs to the Missouri River Valley branch of the Siouan languages. The Crow autonym is *Apsáalooke* or *Absaroka*, a name that means “children of the large-beaked bird” and was given by the Hidatsa. French interpreters translated the name as *gens du corbeau*, meaning “people of the crow” or raven, and English usage became “Crow.”

The sources describe sacred tobacco, visions, medicine, the Sun Dance, and the mythical Thunderbird. Many Apsáalooké people believe that the bird referenced in the tribal name was the mythical Thunderbird, although the identity of the original bird is described as lost to time.
